clue.text: Overtaking in the field

parts.note: read as 'taking an over' while one's team is out in the field at cricket, which describes delivering the ball rather than passing someone

explanation.surface: A runner or rider gets past rivals out in a field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overtaking' suggests passing someone; split it as 'over-taking': in cricket a bowler delivers an over of six balls while their side is fielding.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the fielding side's bowler delivers each over, so taking an over is the act of delivering the ball.

clue.text: Support the other one, clairvoyant initially foretelling events

parts.note: to support is to prop

indicators.note: other asks for a different version of the little word the, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word clairvoyant

explanation.surface: Back up the other person, because a clairvoyant was the first to predict what would happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'other' rearranges THE to HET.
explanation.definitionFit: Something prophetic predicts the future, which is what foretelling events means.

clue.text: Some brazen analogy about harem in India

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A rather shameless comparison is drawn concerning an Indian harem.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition included 'about', but the Indian word means the harem itself, so 'about' is only a link word between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The zenana is the secluded women's quarters of a household in India, the equivalent of a harem.

clue.text: Revised offer Pat made for contract

indicators.note: a revised offer has been reworked, so the letters of offer and Pat are rearranged

explanation.surface: Pat drew up a changed bid for a business contract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contract' looks like a noun for a deal; here it is the verb, to narrow or dwindle.
explanation.definitionFit: To taper off is to dwindle or narrow gradually, a sense of the verb contract.

clue.text: How one in bed had some medicine?

definitions.text: How one in bed had some medicine?

parts.words: How one in bed had some medicine?
parts.note: a patient lying in bed would swallow a dose while horizontal; the phrase also means accepting a setback meekly

explanation.surface: A bedridden patient's way of swallowing a dose.
explanation.walkthrough: The literal reading is a patient horizontal in bed; the idiom means accepting an insult or defeat without protest.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes submitting meekly, and literally describes swallowing a dose while horizontal.

clue.text: Reputed set had meal about four

parts.note: to set something down is to put it

indicators.note: about means the eating word goes around the numeral for four

parts.note: had a meal means ate
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A supposedly well-known group sat down to eat at about four o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set' and 'had meal' both read as past-tense verbs in the surface, which hides the plain verb PUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Putative and reputed both mean commonly supposed or believed to be so.

clue.text: Get knotted again

parts.note: the rude dismissal 'get knotted' is read literally as an instruction to tie a knot once more

explanation.surface: A rude brush-off told to someone for a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get knotted' is British slang for 'go away'; taken literally it means fasten in a knot.
explanation.definitionFit: To fasten a knot a second time is to do up a lace or string once more.

clue.text: Resort in front in chaos

indicators.note: in chaos means the letters of front and in are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A seaside resort's promenade is in disarray.
explanation.walkthrough: FRINTON-on-Sea is a quiet seaside resort in Essex, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Frinton-on-Sea is an English seaside town that holidaymakers visit, a resort.

clue.text: Book supplying information on river's starting-point

explanation.surface: A reference work describes where a river begins.
explanation.definitionFit: A reference used for facts is a source, and a stream's spring or origin is also called its source.

clue.text: Barely beat one's opponents

parts.note: barely suggests narrowly, but read it as naked: beating rivals at undressing

explanation.surface: Someone scrapes a narrow win over their rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely' seems to mean 'only just'; it hints at stripping off. To outstrip is simply to surpass.
explanation.definitionFit: To surpass or get ahead of competitors is to leave them behind, and the split reading is to excel at undressing.

clue.text: Man getting behind part of the aircraft for a biscuit

indicators.note: getting behind means the man's name is placed after the aircraft part

parts.note: a flap is a hinged section of an aircraft's wing
Jack is a man's name

explanation.surface: A fellow climbs into the rear of a plane to fetch a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: A British FLAPJACK is an oat-and-syrup bar, which explains 'biscuit'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a flapjack is a chewy oat bar eaten as a sweet snack, loosely a biscuit.

clue.text: Score double ten

explanation.surface: A tally reached by doubling ten.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is an old word for a group of twenty, which is also twice ten.

clue.text: Behave with one another to cover part of the play

parts.note: to inter is to bury, covering with earth
an act is a division of a stage play

explanation.surface: Actors must get along while covering one section of a drama.
explanation.definitionFit: To interact is to act on or communicate with each other, mutual behaviour.

clue.text: Nothing performed for sweetheart

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring
performed means done

explanation.surface: No act was put on for the person one adores.
explanation.definitionFit: A dear partner or beloved person is a cherished companion, as a sweetheart is.

clue.text: Sign on letter to help retrograde fault-finder

indicators.note: retrograde means moving backwards, so the word for help is read in reverse

parts.note: help means aid
a critic is someone who finds fault

explanation.surface: A backward-looking critic is asked to help with a sign on a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retrograde' turns AID into DIA.
explanation.definitionFit: An accent such as a cedilla or umlaut is a mark added to a letter, a diacritic.

clue.text: Commander having drinks before this French get together

parts.note: CO stands for commanding officer
ales are drinks of beer
ce is French for this

explanation.surface: An officer has a few beers before joining a French party.
explanation.definitionFit: To coalesce is to merge or unite, coming together into one.

clue.text: Brother has awful colic, from greens!

indicators.note: awful suggests the letters of colic are in a bad state and rearranged

explanation.surface: A sibling has terrible stomach pains after eating vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges COLIC to CCOLI.
explanation.definitionFit: Broccoli is a green vegetable, and greens means such leafy vegetables.

clue.text: Drive off successfully

parts.note: suggests a golfer teeing off well, but means to beat back an attacking force

explanation.surface: A golfer hits a good tee shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive off' hints at golf; the sense is fighting off an attacker.
explanation.definitionFit: To beat back an attack and force the enemy away is to repel it.

clue.text: Release a Parisian before tea has arrived

parts.note: un is French for a, as spoken in Paris
cha is a slang word for tea
a train that has arrived is in

explanation.surface: A Frenchman frees someone before the tea is served.
explanation.definitionFit: To unchain someone is to free them from fetters, setting them loose.

clue.text: Being observant when it is thawing?

explanation.surface: Spotting things while the frost melts.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer as NOT ICING: when it thaws, water is not freezing.
explanation.definitionFit: Being observant means paying attention and spotting things, and thawing weather is when ice is not forming.

clue.text: Test score released

parts.note: a try is a score in rugby
released means out, as a prisoner let free

explanation.surface: A trial of a scoring system is made public.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby a TRY is a score made by grounding the ball over the line.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryout is a trial or audition to test someone's ability.

clue.text: Fielders' petition

parts.note: fielders at cricket shout to the umpire asking for a batsman to be given out

explanation.surface: The fielding team asks the umpire for a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the fielders call 'Howzat?' to request a dismissal from the umpire.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal request or plea, like a cricketer's shout to the umpire, is an appeal.

clue.text: Bird could get about inside

indicators.note: inside means the word for about goes within the rearranged letters
could hints that the letters of get might be arranged differently

parts.note: taken as written
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: A bird might be able to fly around within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could' is an unusual anagram signal: the letters could be otherwise arranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The egret is a white heron, a wading bird.

clue.text: Robbery that's blatant overcharging

parts.note: describes the British idiom for a shameless price, robbery done in full view rather than at night

explanation.surface: A complaint about a shop's outrageous prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daylight robbery' is the British idiom for a grossly excessive price.
explanation.definitionFit: Theft committed openly is done in broad sunlight, hence the idiom for blatant overcharging.

clue.text: A pupil takes mural into the open-air

parts.note: L is a learner, as on a British learner driver's plate
a fresco is a painting on a wall

explanation.surface: A student carries a wall painting outdoors.
explanation.walkthrough: L for learner comes from the L-plates new drivers display in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Done outdoors, under the sky, as an al fresco meal is.

clue.text: One in Paris provided some of the diamonds making one

parts.note: un is French for one
if means provided that

indicators.note: some of means only part of the slang word is used, its final letter dropped

parts.note: ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: A Parisian, if given a few of the gems, would be unified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some of' trims ICE to IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Unific means unifying, causing things to become a single whole.

clue.text: Lear goes round the North as if tanned

indicators.note: goes round means the name Lear encloses the word the

parts.note: taken as written, the king from Shakespeare
taken as written

explanation.surface: King Lear travels around the north and looks sunburnt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as if tanned' is a slightly loose definition: leathern means made of or like leather, tanned hide.
explanation.definitionFit: Leathern means made of leather, which is tanned hide.
